opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's one where I think people sometimes look at the wrong number. The headline figure everyone wants is the raw cost comparison: what does it cost to have a human annotator draw boxes or masks on a million images, versus running a foundation model to produce those labels automatically? And in our experiments, that gap is enormous, several orders of magnitude cheaper and dramatically faster. You can label a dataset in hours on a single GPU that would have taken a team of annotators weeks or months.

But that's only half the story. The real way to assess value is to ask: what does the downstream model look like when trained on those auto-generated labels, compared to one trained on human labels? Because labels aren't the product. The model is the product. So what we tried to do was hold the training pipeline fixed, swap in auto-labels versus human labels, and measure performance on a held-out validation set that was carefully human-annotated.

What we found was surprising to a lot of people, including me to some degree. For many common object detection settings, models trained on auto-labels got remarkably close to, and in some configurations essentially matched, models trained on human labels. And there's an interesting subtlety around confidence thresholds. Intuitively you'd crank the threshold up so you only keep labels the model is very sure about. It turns out that's often not optimal. A moderate threshold, which lets in some noise but gives you much better recall, frequently produced better downstream models. Missing objects hurts more than a few false positives.

Then you have to factor in the costs that don't show up on the invoice. Human annotation has its own error rates. Annotators get tired, guidelines get interpreted inconsistently, and you spend a lot of time on QA and relabeling cycles. Auto-labeling is consistent, even if consistently wrong in certain ways, and that's arguably easier to diagnose and fix.

So the way I'd frame it: the value isn't "replace humans entirely." It's shifting where human effort goes. Let the models do the bulk first pass on the easy, common classes, and redirect human attention to the hard cases, the rare classes, the ambiguous edge cases, and to curating and auditing the data. That's where human judgment adds the most value per hour. And when you account for that reallocation, plus how fast you can iterate on a dataset, the return is substantial. Iteration speed may be the biggest win of all, because the teams that build the best models are usually the ones who can go through the most data-model improvement loops.

There are caveats. For specialized domains like medical imaging, or classes the foundation models have barely seen, auto-labeling performance drops, and you need humans more heavily in the loop. So my practical advice is to run a small pilot: label a sample both ways, train, compare, and let the numbers on your own data tell you where automated labeling pays off and where it doesn't.

r001.rationale: The response separates the large time and cost savings from effectiveness, which it evaluates by comparing downstream models trained on auto-labels versus human labels on a human-annotated validation set.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that's a question we get a lot, and I think the honest answer is that it depends on what you're actually measuring. The naive way to think about it is, okay, a human annotator costs X dollars an hour, they can label Y frames or Y images in that hour, and if a model can do that same labeling in a fraction of the time, you just multiply it out and there's your savings. And that number can look really compelling. But I think it misses a couple of things.

The first is that the time savings isn't really about the labeling itself, it's about the iteration loop. When I was running research groups, the thing that killed us wasn't the cost of labeling, it was the latency. You'd decide you needed a new attribute, or a new class, or you realized your taxonomy was wrong, and then you'd wait weeks to get data back before you could even find out whether the idea was good. So when you compress that from weeks to hours, the value isn't the dollars you saved on annotators, it's that you get to try ten ideas instead of one. That's a very different kind of value and it's harder to put on a spreadsheet, but I'd argue it's the bigger one.

The second thing is that automated labeling is never really free, because you still have to verify it. If a model produces labels, somebody has to decide how much to trust them, and that trust has to be earned per dataset, per domain. So the realistic workflow isn't "the machine labels everything and we're done," it's that the machine labels everything and then you spend your human budget very deliberately on the parts the model is uncertain about, or the long-tail stuff, or the edge cases where errors are expensive. So the savings are real, but you're redirecting human effort, not eliminating it.

And then the third piece, which I think people underweight, is the quality side. Labeling isn't just a cost center, it's where a lot of your data quality problems originate. Inconsistent annotators, drift in how people interpret guidelines over a long project, that kind of thing. A model, for all its faults, is at least consistent. So part of what you're buying is consistency, and that shows up downstream as a better trained model, not as a line item in the labeling budget.

So when we assess it, we try to look at three things together: the raw throughput and cost, sure, but also how much faster the team can iterate on the problem, and what happens to the error rate of the final model. If you only look at the first one, you'll either overvalue it because the number looks huge, or undervalue it because you forget that the verification still costs something.

r001.rationale: The response separates raw throughput and cost savings from labeling quality and downstream model error rates, and says labels require dataset-specific verification. This distinguishes whether automation is effective from how much time or money it saves.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to look at the total effort required to get to a dataset you can actually train on. It’s easy to say, “The system generated these labels in a few seconds, so look how much time we saved.” But if a person then has to review every label and correct a lot of them, that changes the calculation.

So I would compare the manual workflow with the automated workflow at the same level of quality. How much human time goes into creating, reviewing, and correcting the annotations? And ultimately, does that dataset produce the model performance you need? The savings are valuable when they reduce that whole cycle—when your team can get to a useful model faster, or explore more iterations with the same budget.

r001.rationale: The response separates speed and cost savings from effectiveness by asking whether the resulting dataset achieves the needed model performance, and notes that review and correction can erode the apparent savings.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to look beyond the cost per annotation and ask how it changes the overall model development cycle. If I can get a useful labeled dataset sooner, I can train a model, understand where it fails, and use that information to decide what to label next. That faster feedback loop can be more valuable than the direct savings on labeling.

But quality has to be part of that calculation. If automation produces labels that require extensive correction, you've shifted the work rather than saved it. So I would compare the human effort required to reach a given level of model performance, including review and correction. The goal is to use automation where it works well and focus people's attention on the examples that actually need their judgment.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes savings from effectiveness by emphasizing label quality, correction effort, and the human effort needed to reach a given model performance.
